Reference: Allen and Donaldson (2022)

Model Setting

The paper asks how much of today's spatial distribution of economic activity is determined by history and not by geographic fundamentals, how long a temporary local shock should be expected to affect local economic concentration, and when such a shock has permanent consequences. It builds a deliberately simple dynamic model of economic geography with an arbitrary number of heterogeneous locations that interact through migration, with agglomeration externalities in production and in amenities and with endogenous fertility. The model is a primer on Allen and Donaldson (2020). When locations interact through trade and migration, the equilibrium is a system of equations with a block structure, one block for each source of interaction across locations, and the earlier paper has four blocks. Two simplifications reduce the system to one block in the vector of local populations. First, there are no trade costs and all locations produce one homogeneous good, which removes the block that determines nominal wages from exports and the block that determines the cost of living from imports. Second, parents have more children when those children expect high lifetime welfare, and under one parameter restriction this force exactly offsets the usual tendency of attractive origins to send out fewer migrants, which merges the two migration blocks (attractiveness as a destination and as a birthplace) into one.

Three terms organize the analysis. Multiplicity means that the transition from one period to the next is indeterminate. Persistence is the slow decay of the effect of a temporary change in historical conditions when the equilibrium is unique. Path dependence means that a temporary change has permanent effects because it moves the economy towards a different steady state. The central message is the distinction between spillovers that affect productivity or amenities contemporaneously and spillovers that act with a lag of one generation. There are four results. The dynamic equilibrium is unique and stable when total contemporaneous spillovers are weaker than the dispersion force. Local persistence in partial equilibrium is higher when either contemporaneous or historical spillovers are large. Persistence of the whole economy in general equilibrium is governed by the sum of contemporaneous and historical spillovers. Multiple stable steady states can arise, and for some geographies are guaranteed to arise, when that sum is large. Hence there is a parameter region in which the equilibrium is unique and stable, each location converges in partial equilibrium, and path dependence is nonetheless possible. A back-of-the-envelope reading of estimates in the literature places a typical economy in this region. The paper contains no simulation or formal calibration.

Production

There is a finite number of locations iii and of periods ttt. Agents live for two periods in overlapping generations, childhood and adulthood. Each location produces, under perfect competition, a nationally homogeneous and freely traded good with local adult labour only. Producer ϕ\phiϕ has the linear technology yit(ϕ)=Aitlit(ϕ)y_{it}(\phi)=A_{it}l_{it}(\phi)yit​(ϕ)=Ait​lit​(ϕ) and charges the price pit(ϕ)=1p_{it}(\phi)=1pit​(ϕ)=1 by choice of numeraire, so the nominal and real wage is wit=Aitw_{it}=A_{it}wit​=Ait​. Producers take productivity as given, but it depends on the total local adult population Lit≡∑ϕlit(ϕ)L_{it}\equiv\sum_{\phi}l_{it}(\phi)Lit​≡∑ϕ​lit​(ϕ):

Ait=AˉitLitα1Li,t−1α2(1)A_{it}=\bar{A}_{it}L_{it}^{\alpha_1}L_{i,t-1}^{\alpha_2} \tag{1}Ait​=Aˉit​Litα1​​Li,t−1α2​​(1)

where Aˉit\bar{A}_{it}Aˉit​ is an arbitrary exogenous productivity, α1\alpha_1α1​ is the elasticity of the contemporaneous spillover and α2\alpha_2α2​ is the elasticity of the historical spillover, through which the lagged population of a location affects its current productivity. Both can be positive or negative. The form is reduced: a negative α1\alpha_1α1​ could simply reflect omitted capital or land, and a positive α2\alpha_2α2​ stands for past investments that remain productive. Microfoundations mentioned by the paper include innovating firms that hold a patent in period ttt, face competition in t+1t+1t+1 and see the product become obsolete in t+2t+2t+2 (Deneckere and Judd 1992), and endogenous innovation with contemporaneous scale effects and lagged spatial diffusion (Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg 2014). Richer processes, such as immobile capital that decays over several periods, would add further lags such as Li,t−2L_{i,t-2}Li,t−2​ in the same isoelastic form. The inverse labour demand of a location follows directly:

ln⁡wit=α1ln⁡Lit+α2ln⁡Li,t−1+ln⁡Aˉit(2)\ln w_{it}=\alpha_1\ln L_{it}+\alpha_2\ln L_{i,t-1}+\ln\bar{A}_{it} \tag{2}lnwit​=α1​lnLit​+α2​lnLi,t−1​+lnAˉit​(2)

The labour demand curve slopes upward whenever α1\alpha_1α1​ is positive.

Phase Diagrams

The concepts are first illustrated with a generic economy of two locations, summarized by the share λt∈[0,1]\lambda_t\in[0,1]λt​∈[0,1] of total population in location one and a scalar mapping λt+1=f(λt)\lambda_{t+1}=f(\lambda_t)λt+1​=f(λt​) that also depends on the fundamentals and on Θ≡(α1,α2,β1,β2,θ)\Theta\equiv(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\beta_1,\beta_2,\theta)Θ≡(α1​,α2​,β1​,β2​,θ). Total population is endogenous in the model, so two equilibria with the same shares need not have the same level. The diagrams abstract from this and the propositions do not. Six phase diagrams plot λt+1\lambda_{t+1}λt+1​ against λt\lambda_tλt​ with the 45-degree line.

  • Uniqueness: in panel (a) fff is single-valued, so every initial condition has one successor. In panel (b) fff is multi-valued (two horizontal branches, at zero and at one), so the transition is indeterminate.

  • Persistence: in panels (c) and (d) fff is single-valued and upward-sloping with slope below one, and it crosses the 45-degree line from above, so there is one stable steady state λSS\lambda^{SS}λSS. In (c) the mapping is nearly flat and the economy converges quickly from any starting point. In (d) the slope approaches one from below and a shock to λt\lambda_tλt​ leaves a visible trace for many periods.

  • Path dependence: in panel (e) there is one stable steady state. In panel (f) the mapping is S-shaped and crosses the 45-degree line three times, with stable steady states λASS\lambda^{SS}_AλASS​ and λCSS\lambda^{SS}_CλCSS​ and an unstable one λBSS\lambda^{SS}_BλBSS​ between them. An economy that starts below λBSS\lambda^{SS}_BλBSS​ settles at λASS\lambda^{SS}_AλASS​ and one that starts above settles at λCSS\lambda^{SS}_CλCSS​. A temporary shock that moves λt\lambda_tλt​ across λBSS\lambda^{SS}_BλBSS​ therefore changes the long-run outcome permanently. Multiple steady states are a necessary condition for path dependence.

Uniqueness of the Dynamic Equilibrium

Proposition 1 states that if θ(α1+β1)≠1\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1)\neq1θ(α1​+β1​)=1, then for any initial population distribution {Li0}\{L_{i0}\}{Li0​} and any geography with positive Aˉit\bar{A}_{it}Aˉit​, uˉit\bar{u}_{it}uˉit​ and μijt\mu_{ijt}μijt​ there exists a unique equilibrium. The proof is immediate: the right-hand side of the equilibrium relation contains only exogenous and predetermined variables, so the relation can be solved for LitL_{it}Lit​ location by location and iterated forward from t=1t=1t=1. As θ(α1+β1)\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1)θ(α1​+β1​) approaches one from below, LitL_{it}Lit​ becomes infinitely responsive to the right-hand side and all population would agglomerate in the location with the best fundamentals. The same argument applies to any other location, and these black hole equilibria of complete concentration are the root of multiplicity, which occurs only at the knife edge. If θ(α1+β1)>1\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1)>1θ(α1​+β1​)>1 the equilibrium is again unique, but worse locations have larger populations, so that their stronger agglomeration exactly offsets their inferior fundamentals. That equilibrium is unstable, in the sense that moving people away from the inferior locations would make those people better off. The paper therefore focuses on the condition θ(α1+β1)<1\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1)<1θ(α1​+β1​)<1, which guarantees a unique and stable equilibrium. Since θ>1\theta>1θ>1, it always holds when net contemporaneous spillovers are negative. Otherwise it requires contemporaneous agglomeration α1+β1\alpha_1+\beta_1α1​+β1​ to be weaker than dispersion 1/θ1/\theta1/θ. The condition does not involve α2\alpha_2α2​ or β2\beta_2β2​, because every generation takes the lagged population distribution as given.

Persistence in Partial Equilibrium

Taking logs of the equilibrium relation:

This is a first-order autoregressive process for the log population of each location. The first term is the exogenous component, and the third term, which has a migration market access form, carries all interactions across regions. Partial equilibrium here means holding the third term constant, which is coherent when there are many small regions, so that the mechanical contribution of a location to its own access term is negligible. The effect of a ceteris paribus increase in ln⁡Li,t−1\ln L_{i,t-1}lnLi,t−1​ is then the partial equilibrium AR(1) coefficient:

ρPE≡θ(α2+β2)1−θ(α1+β1)(16)\rho^{PE}\equiv\frac{\theta(\alpha_2+\beta_2)}{1-\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1)} \tag{16}ρPE≡1−θ(α1​+β1​)θ(α2​+β2​)​(16)

In the region with a unique stable equilibrium the denominator is positive. As θ(α1+β1)\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1)θ(α1​+β1​) approaches one from below, ρPE\rho^{PE}ρPE grows without bound: the closer the parameters are to the threshold of non-uniqueness, the greater the persistence. The numerator shows the role of historical spillovers. If α2+β2\alpha_2+\beta_2α2​+β2​ is positive then ρPE\rho^{PE}ρPE is positive, and nothing rules out ρPE>1\rho^{PE}>1ρPE>1, in which case the partial equilibrium dynamics diverge. Divergence is excluded when ρPE<1\rho^{PE}<1ρPE<1, that is, when:

θ(α1+β1+α2+β2)<1(17)\theta\left(\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2\right)<1 \tag{17}θ(α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​)<1(17)

Persistence is thus greater when net contemporaneous spillovers are large, when net historical spillovers are large, and when dispersion is weak (θ\thetaθ is large). The paper notes that estimating ρPE\rho^{PE}ρPE from a regression of this form must control for market access and for unobserved fundamentals, and that measurement error makes LitL_{it}Lit​ and Li,t−1L_{i,t-1}Li,t−1​ negatively correlated.

where ρGE\rho^{GE}ρGE is the general equilibrium AR(1) coefficient. θ(α1+β1+α2+β2)<0(21)\theta\left(\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2\right)<0 \tag{21}θ(α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​)<0(21)

Total net agglomeration forces must be negative. On any transition path the gap between the rate of change of the fastest-changing and the slowest-changing location then shrinks every period. Since ρGE>ρPE\rho^{GE}>\rho^{PE}ρGE>ρPE, the economy as a whole can be more persistent than the partial equilibrium evolution of any single location. The partial equilibrium coefficient can be below one while the general equilibrium bound exceeds one, which the paper suggests as a possible source of the differences in estimated speeds of convergence across empirical studies: some settings approximate the partial equilibrium ideal and others do not.

Steady States and Path Dependence

Path dependence is tied to multiple steady states: a temporary shock has permanent effects only if it moves the economy to a different steady state. Hold the geography constant at {Aˉi>0,uˉi>0,μij>0}\{\bar{A}_i>0,\bar{u}_i>0,\mu_{ij}>0\}{Aˉi​>0,uˉi​>0,μij​>0} and look for constant populations LiL_iLi​ in the equilibrium relation. A steady state satisfies, for every location iii:

Li1−θ(α1+β1+α2+β2)=∑jμji−θ(Aˉiuˉi)θLj(22)L_i^{1-\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2)}=\sum_j\mu_{ji}^{-\theta}\left(\bar{A}_i\bar{u}_i\right)^{\theta}L_j \tag{22}Li1−θ(α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​)​=j∑​μji−θ​(Aˉi​uˉi​)θLj​(22)

This is an instance of a well-studied nonlinear system:

zi=∑jKijzjγ,zi≡Li1−θ(α1+β1+α2+β2),γ≡11−θ(α1+β1+α2+β2)(23)z_i=\sum_jK_{ij}z_j^{\gamma},\qquad z_i\equiv L_i^{1-\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2)},\qquad\gamma\equiv\frac{1}{1-\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2)} \tag{23}zi​=j∑​Kij​zjγ​,zi​≡Li1−θ(α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​)​,γ≡1−θ(α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​)1​(23)

where the kernel KijK_{ij}Kij​ collects the migration costs and fundamentals. Such a system is known to have a unique solution if ∣γ∣<1|\gamma|<1∣γ∣<1 (Karlin and Nirenberg 1967; Allen and Arkolakis 2014). Proposition 3 follows: for any time-invariant geography there exists a steady-state equilibrium, and it is unique if:

∣11−θ(α1+β1+α2+β2)∣<1(24)\left|\frac{1}{1-\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2)}\right|<1 \tag{24}​1−θ(α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​)1​​<1(24)

If instead the absolute value exceeds one, there exist many geographies with multiple steady states. If it equals one, there is at most one steady state up to scale. Restricting attention to parameters with θ(α1+β1+α2+β2)≤1\theta(\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2)\leq1θ(α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​)≤1, which is also the region of partial equilibrium convergence, the uniqueness condition reduces to α1+β1+α2+β2<0\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2<0α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​<0. The paper makes three comments. First, the condition for a unique steady state is more demanding than the condition for a unique dynamic equilibrium, which needs only α1+β1<1/θ\alpha_1+\beta_1<1/\thetaα1​+β1​<1/θ. Historical spillovers do not affect the choices of agents who take the past as given, but the attraction that history gives a location can be reason enough for each generation to move there, and this behaviour can become a self-fulfilling resting place for the economy. Second, the condition for a unique steady state coincides with the condition for uniform convergence. This need not hold in general dynamic systems. Here, net dispersive total spillovers guarantee both a single steady state and uniform convergence to it from every initial condition. Third, the condition is sufficient for every geography and cannot be necessary at that level of generality, but it is the weakest such general condition, because geographies with multiple steady states always exist when it is violated. Examples exist with as few as two locations, and Allen and Donaldson (2020) show a continuum of examples with four locations in the presence of trade costs.

Parameter Regions

The results are summarized in a diagram with the net contemporaneous spillover α1+β1\alpha_1+\beta_1α1​+β1​ on the horizontal axis and the net historical spillover α2+β2\alpha_2+\beta_2α2​+β2​ on the vertical axis. Two boundaries matter: the vertical line α1+β1=1/θ\alpha_1+\beta_1=1/\thetaα1​+β1​=1/θ and the downward-sloping line α1+β1+α2+β2=0\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2=0α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​=0, together with its parallel shift to 1/θ1/\theta1/θ.

  • Right of the vertical line: with α1+β1>1/θ\alpha_1+\beta_1>1/\thetaα1​+β1​>1/θ the equilibrium is unique but unstable. Multiplicity (the black hole) occurs only on the line itself.

  • Purple region: with α1+β1<1/θ\alpha_1+\beta_1<1/\thetaα1​+β1​<1/θ and α1+β1+α2+β2<0\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2<0α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​<0 the equilibrium is unique and stable, convergence is uniform in general equilibrium, the steady state is unique and there is no path dependence.

  • Green region: with α1+β1<1/θ\alpha_1+\beta_1<1/\thetaα1​+β1​<1/θ and 0<α1+β1+α2+β2<1/θ0<\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2<1/\theta0<α1​+β1​+α2​+β2​<1/θ the equilibrium is unique and stable and each location converges in partial equilibrium, but uniform convergence is not guaranteed and multiple steady states, hence path dependence, are possible.

  • Blue region: with α1+β1<1/θ\alpha_1+\beta_1<1/\thetaα1​+β1​<1/θ and α1+β1+α2+β2>1/θ\alpha_1+\beta_1+\alpha_2+\beta_2>1/\thetaα1​+β1​+α2​+β2​>1/θ the equilibrium is unique and stable, but even partial equilibrium convergence is not guaranteed, and path dependence is possible.

Within the stable region, ρPE=(α2+β2)/[1θ−(α1+β1)]\rho^{PE}=(\alpha_2+\beta_2)/[\frac{1}{\theta}-(\alpha_1+\beta_1)]ρPE=(α2​+β2​)/[θ1​−(α1​+β1​)], so historical spillovers are scaled up as contemporaneous spillovers approach 1/θ1/\theta1/θ from below. A particularly rich and still tractable case has negative contemporaneous spillovers and historical spillovers large enough to make the sum positive: the dynamic equilibrium is unique and stable, yet steady states can be multiple.

Together with the two migration blocks this is a four-block system. With symmetric trade costs, τijt=τjit\tau_{ijt}=\tau_{jit}τijt​=τjit​, the two trade blocks collapse into one. Uniqueness conditions then depend on the spectral radius of a matrix of coefficients whose size equals the number of blocks.

Third, adults may live until the economy ends after TTT periods and be forward-looking throughout. The single-period payoff in the migration probability is replaced by the value of remaining life in location iii at time ttt:

Vit=WitΠi,t+1δ(27)V_{it}=W_{it}\Pi_{i,t+1}^{\delta} \tag{27}Vit​=Wit​Πi,t+1δ​(27)

Raising δ\deltaδ from zero, its implicit value in the simple model, shifts the purple and blue regions inwards: different expectations about future spatial configurations can become self-fulfilling with weaker spillovers when the future matters more, the force stressed by Krugman (1991) and Matsuyama (1991).

αˉ1≡max⁡i,Litdln⁡fi(Lit)dln⁡Lit(28)\bar{\alpha}_1\equiv\max_{i,L_{it}}\frac{d\ln f_i(L_{it})}{d\ln L_{it}} \tag{28}αˉ1​≡i,Lit​max​dlnLit​dlnfi​(Lit​)​(28)

This covers the urban tradition in which increasing returns are eventually overcome by congestion. In the baseline model city sizes are interior, even with α1+β1>0\alpha_1+\beta_1>0α1​+β1​>0, because of the dispersion created by preference heterogeneity.

Estimation and Back-of-the-Envelope Quantification

Locating an economy in the diagram requires separate estimates of the contemporaneous spillovers (α1\alpha_1α1​, β1\beta_1β1​) and of the historical spillovers (α2\alpha_2α2​, β2\beta_2β2​), and the latter have received much less attention, especially at a lag of one generation. The paper proposes an extension of the Rosen-Roback tradition that treats the inverse labour demand and labour supply equations as estimating equations with data on witw_{it}wit​, LitL_{it}Lit​ and Li,t−1L_{i,t-1}Li,t−1​. In the demand equation Aˉit\bar{A}_{it}Aˉit​ is unobserved and wages and populations are jointly determined, so ordinary least squares is biased even if Aˉit\bar{A}_{it}Aˉit​ is purely exogenous. Valid instruments shift supply but are excluded from demand: observed characteristics that affect amenities uˉit\bar{u}_{it}uˉit​ and not productivity, observable components of migration frictions μijt\mu_{ijt}μijt​, and current or lagged productivity and amenities of other locations. One caveat is that an inflow of workers to high-amenity places may raise land prices and lead firms to substitute from land to labour, which changes labour productivity. In the supply equation uˉit\bar{u}_{it}uˉit​ is unobserved and observed shifters of Aˉit\bar{A}_{it}Aˉit​ can serve as instruments. Here ln⁡IMMAit\ln IMMA_{it}lnIMMAit​ must be controlled for, and its coefficient identifies θ\thetaθ, which is needed to recover β1\beta_1β1​ from the coefficient on ln⁡Lit\ln L_{it}lnLit​. The bilateral migration shares offer another route to θ\thetaθ. The authors are not aware of estimates of the two equations in this form.

The numerical illustration uses values from the literature. Typical estimates of production spillovers span 0.03 to 0.08. They correspond to α1\alpha_1α1​ when Li,t−1L_{i,t-1}Li,t−1​ is controlled for or orthogonal to LitL_{it}Lit​, and to α1+α2\alpha_1+\alpha_2α1​+α2​ when the economy is close to a steady state. The amenity spillover β1\beta_1β1​ can stand for unmodeled immobile local goods in fixed supply, such as land, which suggests a negative value, and β2\beta_2β2​ is then positive if past investments in such factors are still durable a generation later. For the migration elasticity, Monte, Redding and Rossi-Hansberg (2018) obtain θ=3.30\theta=3.30θ=3.30, although not for moves between generations. The paper then supposes that α1+α2=0.08\alpha_1+\alpha_2=0.08α1​+α2​=0.08, that contemporaneous amenity spillovers come from housing with about one third of expenditure, so β1=−0.33\beta_1=-0.33β1​=−0.33, and that housing is approximately fully durable over a generation, so β2=0.33\beta_2=0.33β2​=0.33. Then α1+α2+β1+β2=0.08>0\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\beta_1+\beta_2=0.08>0α1​+α2​+β1​+β2​=0.08>0. If in addition both productivity spillovers are non-negative, or simply α1<0.41\alpha_1<0.41α1​<0.41, the economy lies in the green region, with a unique and stable equilibrium and partial equilibrium convergence but scope for path dependence, for any θ\thetaθ below 12.5 (the value at which the total spillover of 0.08 equals 1/θ1/\theta1/θ). In the conclusion the authors add that when steady states are multiple they generally differ in aggregate welfare, and they raise the question of Rauch (1993) whether history matters only when it matters little, since large heterogeneity in fundamentals may be exactly what rules out multiple steady states.

This is the assumed productivity technology of location iii in period ttt, a primitive of the model. AitA_{it}Ait​ is output per adult worker, Aˉit>0\bar{A}_{it}>0Aˉit​>0 is the exogenous part (soil, climate, access to the coast, anything not caused by population), LitL_{it}Lit​ is the current adult population and Li,t−1L_{i,t-1}Li,t−1​ is the adult population one generation earlier. The two exponents are elasticities:

α1=∂ln⁡Ait∂ln⁡Lit,α2=∂ln⁡Ait∂ln⁡Li,t−1\alpha_1=\frac{\partial\ln A_{it}}{\partial\ln L_{it}},\qquad\alpha_2=\frac{\partial\ln A_{it}}{\partial\ln L_{i,t-1}}α1​=∂lnLit​∂lnAit​​,α2​=∂lnLi,t−1​∂lnAit​​

The contemporaneous spillover α1\alpha_1α1​ is positive under standard agglomeration economies and negative when an omitted fixed factor (land, capital) makes labour less productive as it crowds in. The historical spillover α2\alpha_2α2​ lets the size of the previous generation matter today, for instance through durable infrastructure or knowledge left behind. Both are external to the individual producer, who treats AitA_{it}Ait​ as a constant, so that perfect competition survives even when α1>0\alpha_1>0α1​>0.

The isoelastic (log-linear) form is what makes the whole model tractable: after taking logs it yields the linear labour demand of equation (2), and combined with the amenity function of equation (3) it gives the power-function equilibrium relation of equation (14), in which only the sums α1+β1\alpha_1+\beta_1α1​+β1​ and α2+β2\alpha_2+\beta_2α2​+β2​ matter. It rules out spillovers that change sign with city size, a case treated in equation (28). As an illustration, with α1=0.05\alpha_1=0.05α1​=0.05 a doubling of LitL_{it}Lit​ raises productivity by the factor 20.05≈1.0352^{0.05}\approx1.03520.05≈1.035, that is, by about 3.5 per cent.

The logic is that uniqueness and convergence arguments are contraction arguments such as the one behind equation (24), and a contraction requires a bound on the response of the map everywhere, which is given by the worst-case elasticity.
